Tesla has been busy reshaping its business around robotaxis, humanoid robots and energy projects while the share price has swung sharply, and that leaves a basic question for you as an investor. Is the current US$345.82 price tag adequately backed by what the company is generating through its sales today?

Over the past 3 years the stock has gained 46.9%, which puts a lot of weight on whether recent top line performance can carry that kind of market value.

A planned €3b expansion of the Berlin Gigafactory for Cybercab production, along with large new projects in chips and solar, can reshape future revenue but also means heavier near term spending that matters for how you think about sales based valuation.

Your read on Tesla is one view; the desks covering it have another. See what analysts think Tesla's shares could be worth.

The issue now is whether Tesla's current share price is justified by its sales once you line it up against the Fair Ratio benchmark.

If you are weighing Tesla's US$345.82 share price against its current sales, it can help to see how other companies tied to AI infrastructure are valued through our 53 AI infrastructure stocks.

Does Tesla Look Pricey on Sales?

P/S is a useful lens for Tesla because so much of the story revolves around what each dollar of revenue could one day be worth rather than today's accounting earnings. On this metric, the stock trades on a P/S of 13.2x, compared with an auto industry average of 0.4x and a peer group around 1.1x. Investors are therefore paying a much richer tag for every unit of current sales than is typical in the sector.

The Fair Ratio, which adjusts for Tesla's growth profile, margins, size and risk, indicates that this P/S level screens as overvalued, and the gap is wide enough that the model functions more as a warning signal than a precise target. Despite the fresh wave of capital intensive projects in robotaxis, chips and solar, along with the planned €3b Berlin expansion, the current P/S still reflects very high expectations for what those ventures will eventually deliver in revenue terms. ARK Invest founder, CEO, and Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood stated her firm used the recent market pullback to purchase shares of Nvidia Corp., Tesla Inc., and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., while noting that cyclical technology and memory stocks fell sharply.

Concentrating on High-Conviction Technology

Wood told Wolf Financial Show host Goff Blackburg that ARK Invest sees "opportunity everywhere" following the recent technology sector sell-off. Wood stated that the firm responded to the market movement by altering its portfolio, explaining, "we concentrated our holdings towards our highest conviction names."

Wood specified that ARK Invest recently purchased shares in multiple technology companies. "We bought Tesla and SpaceX, we added to AMD, but we also added to Nvidia," Wood stated.

Wood characterized recent weekend news regarding Nvidia as "quite disappointing," but she pointed to comments from Elon Musk, who Wood quoted as saying, "We're speeding up our data centers in space."

She stated that Nvidia supported these orbital data centers, which she predicted will be a "huge source of demand" that Nvidia has secured with SpaceX in the near term. Furthermore, Wood stated that data center builders will have to "give more to these communities" rather than just taking from them to avoid derailing data center buildouts.

Cyclical Tech Stocks Slaughtered

Addressing the broader semiconductor and cloud markets, Wood noted that memory and cyclical technology stocks saw significant recent price drops.

Wood said that given the "thrashing" these stocks experienced, she would "probably be attracted" to them if she were an investor who traded that specific part of the market. She also stated she does not believe the "American renaissance is over" despite the recent market volatility.

Musk Won't Take Stock Awards "Simply for Merging With SpaceX." Tesla Shareholders Still Have to Vote ©@Omar_Nasif from pixabay via Canva, @Diego Maravilla © 2022 from Diego Maravilla via Canva
Key Takeaways

Elon Musk said at the DealBook Summit that he shouldn't receive Tesla stock awards just for merging Tesla with SpaceX.

That eases a real dilution worry, since his 2025 pay package covers 423.7 million shares, but it's a statement, not a deal term, and the exchange ratio still matters most for Tesla holders.

Analysts expect SpaceX's revenue to reach $338 billion in 2028, more than twice the $146.1 billion they expect from Tesla, while Tesla trades at about 180x forward earnings.

Any merger needs the votes of a majority of Tesla's outstanding shares, and Musk admitted Tesla's vote could fail.

Elon Musk has answered one of the biggest questions hanging over a merger of Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ): what happens to his Tesla pay.

At the New York Times' DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, Andrew Ross Sorkin asked him whether he should get his Tesla pay award, which is tied to Tesla's own operating targets, if the companies merge.

Musk's response? Referring to awards "contingent upon Tesla execution," he said, "I should not receive those stock option awards simply for merging with SpaceX."

That leaves Tesla holders with the harder question of what a deal would actually pay them.

The award is no small thing

The package Tesla shareholders approved in November 2025 covers 423.7 million shares, about 12% of the 3.53 billion diluted shares Tesla averaged in 2025. Each of its 12 tranches normally requires both a market-value milestone, from $2 trillion to $8.5 trillion, and an operational goal such as 20 million vehicles delivered. Over the last five years, Tesla's diluted share count has gone up only slowly:

Tesla (TSLA): diluted shares outstanding, billions of shares, fiscal 2021-2025 (TIKR)

The award alone is about 3x the 140 million shares that count added from 2021 to 2025. Under its terms, if a deal counts as a change in control, the operational goals drop out and shares can be earned on market value alone. A merger that let Musk collect shares that way would have cost Tesla holders plenty.

Key Takeaways

Trump's September trading report shows up to $380,000 of Nvidia buys, plus Tesla and SpaceX, and sales of $1 million to $5 million each of Home Depot and McDonald's.

The White House says outside firms run the portfolio, and most of the month's money went into a dividend ETF and municipal bonds.

Nvidia trades at about 10x forward earnings, the bottom of its five-year range, against 22x for Home Depot and 21x for McDonald's.

Huang's closed-door House interview on Dec. 1 is the next test for the stock.

President Donald Trump called Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) "such a tragedy" this week. His newest disclosure shows his portfolio added $152,004 to $380,000 of the stock in September.

It also bought Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) and sold blocks of Home Depot (HD:NYSE) and McDonald's (MCD:NYSE). The White House says Trump didn't direct any of it.

TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Nvidia. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

The trades, by the numbers

Trump called Huang "such a brilliant man" in an interview with Fox News that aired Nov. 18. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and on Nov. 17 Nvidia's board chair said the board does not intend to reinstate him.

The Office of Government Ethics released Trump's September trading report on Nov. 19. It lists 751 transactions, and these are the ones that touch the five stocks:

Nvidia: four purchases worth $152,004 to $380,000, two of them on Sept. 2, and a sale of up to $15,000 on Sept. 24

Tesla: early-September purchases, the largest worth $100,001 to $250,000 on Sept. 1

SpaceX: two stock purchases worth $16,002 to $65,000 in all, plus $100,001 to $250,000 of its 5.35% notes due 2031

Home Depot and McDonald's: sales of $1,000,001 to $5 million each, both on Sept. 23

Most of the money went to dividends and bonds

The AI buys are small change next to the rest of the month. The single biggest trade was a purchase of $5 million to $25 million of the Vanguard Dividend Appreciation ETF. The account also bought nearly 100 municipal bonds worth at least $18 million in the first half of September.

The White House says third-party firms manage the portfolio, and that neither Trump nor his family has any say in what it buys or sells. The pattern looks like a manager rebalancing a big account, so none of these trades reads as Trump's call on a stock.

Popular tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee, better known as MKBHD, is following through on a long-running bet involving Tesla Inc.'s (TSLA) Cybercab, after the company opened personal orders for its autonomous vehicle.

Brownlee confirmed he has placed an order for the vehicle, prompting CEO Elon Musk to respond briefly but approvingly on social media.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Tesla shares declined nearly 8% in Friday's regular trading, while gaining about 2% in the afterhours session.

MKBHD Says He'll Follow Through On His Cybercab Bet

Brownlee said he intends to honor the spirit of his earlier bet involving Tesla's Cybercab, confirming that he has submitted the deposit and selected Austin, Texas, as his delivery location.

"I will honor the spirit of the bet. I was invited to buy one, so I did. I submitted my $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and I selected the city of Austin, Texas," Brownlee said in a recent episode of the Waveform podcast.

He added that he would personally travel to Austin if Tesla is ready to deliver the vehicle.

"So if they actually go, 'alright, your Cybercab is ready', I will fly down to Austin, and I will accept delivery of my personal Cybercab," he added.

Musk responded to Brownlee's comments in a post on X with two words, "Fair enough."

The exchange brings the earlier bet back into focus as Tesla begins inviting select customers to purchase the vehicle for personal use, marking a notable step in the company's push toward autonomous transportation.

Tesla Cybercab Personal Orders Come With Restrictions

Tesla recently announced that select customers are being invited to purchase the Cybercab for personal use, with the vehicle priced at an estimated $29,990 and deliveries expected to begin in December.

The offering, however, comes with several restrictions. Buyers must pay a $1,000 non-refundable deposit and a mandatory $299 monthly subscription to operate the vehicle's autonomous driving software.

The Cybercab is a two-seat, two-door vehicle without a steering wheel or pedals, and its personal-use rollout is initially limited to supported geographic areas.

In 2000, Elon Musk Crashed His Uninsured $1 Million McLaren Trying to Show Peter Thiel What It Could Do. In 2025, Thiel’s Fund Quietly Sold Every Tesla Share It Owned

Quick Read

Musk bought the McLaren F1 for about $1 million from his 1999 Zip2 windfall and crashed it on Sand Hill Road in 2000 with Thiel in the passenger seat; it was uninsured, nobody was hurt, and the two hitchhiked to their Sequoia meeting.

Thiel Macro's 13Fs show Tesla as the fund's largest holding on June 30, 2025 (272,613 shares, $86.6 million, 41% of the book); it sold 207,613 shares in the third quarter and the last 65,000 in the fourth, the quarter Tesla set its $489.88 record close.

The fund has reported no Tesla for four straight quarters, including Monday's filing ($460.2 million in five names); at Friday's $345.82 close Tesla is 29% below its record, and the June 2025 stake would be worth $94.3 million, $7.7 million above its filing value.

Founders Fund first backed SpaceX with $20 million in 2008 and its stake was worth more than $50 billion at the June 2026 IPO; Musk now wants to merge Tesla into SpaceX.

In 2000, Elon Musk put Peter Thiel in the passenger seat of a $1 million McLaren F1 he had never insured, floored it on Sand Hill Road to show what the car could do, and crashed it. In 2025, Thiel's hedge fund sold every Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA) share it owned, and its newest filing, sent to the SEC on Monday, shows it still holds none.

Both men have told the crash story themselves. The Tesla sale came with no comment at all, so the filings are the only record. Thiel Macro LLC, the hedge fund that reports Thiel's stock holdings every quarter, cut its Tesla stake by 76% in the third quarter of 2025 and sold the rest in the fourth, the quarter Tesla set its record high. It has reported no Tesla since.
